The bow is held in the dominant hand by its cylindrical end, with the middle finger pressing on it; the hair is stallion horsehair. The three strings are usually tuned in perfect fourths, and the player can use the highest string for the melody and the next as a drone, play the top two together, or use the lowest string for the melody and the next as a drone. The strings are stopped with the fleshy pad of the finger, not the nail; a beginner first practises a steady bow and a clean stop.

黑海克曼琴屬拉弦樂器，源流可追溯至中亞遊牧騎馬文化的兩弦直立拉弦樂器，類似蒙古馬: The Karadeniz kemençe is a bowed instrument whose lineage can be traced to the two-string upright bowed instrument of the nomadic horse-riding culture of Central Asia, similar to the Mongolian morin khuur and the Kazakh kobyz, and possibly related to the horsehair fiddles of the Scythians and the Circassians of the Caucasus. Similar instruments travelled the east–west trade routes into the Middle East and Byzantium; the Iranian kamancheh, the Byzantine lyra and the European rebec are regarded as the direct ancestors of European bowed instruments. The Pontic lyra took shape around the eleventh to twelfth centuries, and the name kemençe is recorded in the tenth century; Pavlos Hieropoulos holds that it was created by the Pontic Greeks. Before 1920 the strings were silk, today they are metal; it has been played historically and now by Turkish and Greek folk musicians.

The Karadeniz kemençe is a traditional bowed chordophone of the Black Sea region of Turkey and Greece, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-71. The body is mostly wooden, commonly with a bottle-like long neck and an oval body, and the three strings are usually tuned in perfect fourths. The player stands or sits with the body upright and pointing down, on the knee when seated and in front of the body when standing, stops the strings with the pad of the finger and bows with a horsehair bow. It is used by Turkish and Greek folk artists, and is also heard accompanying traditional Pontic dance.
